comments.body:
LIVE CONFIRMATION, found by accident while gathering b690's evidence — and it is exactly the failure
mode this ticket describes.

A Bedrock code-review run was configured with `standard = bedrock:us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5`.
That id is INVALID on Bedrock (the valid form carries the version suffix,
`us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0`) — my config error, not a rebar defect. Bedrock
rejected it:

    llm call [code-review-verify] mode=agentic model=bedrock:us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5
    FAILED in 0.5s: status_code: 400 ... {'Error': {'Message': 'The provided model identifier is
    invalid.', 'Code': 'ValidationException'}}

**The usage log for that run contains FIVE rows, all healthy, and NOTHING about the two passes that
failed.** Read the JSONL alone and the run looks like a clean five-call review of `base` + four
Round-A overlays. There is no row for `verify`, no row for `coach`, and no field anywhere saying a
pass was attempted and lost. I only noticed because I happened to read stderr.

That is the concrete cost this ticket is about, demonstrated on a real run rather than argued:
* a reader cannot distinguish "this gate has 5 LLM steps" from "this gate has 7 and 2 failed";
* the per-step attribution b690 just added is silently INCOMPLETE for exactly the runs where
  something went wrong;
* and had the failure been a retry-to-exhaustion rather than an instant 400, the burned input tokens
  would have been invisible to the spend total too.

It also sharpens the acceptance criteria already on this ticket: the failure row needs to name the
step (`verify`) and the class (`standard`) — both were available in the ContextVar at the moment of
failure, since `step_identity` wraps the whole step execution including the raise — so the fix is
about reaching `record()` on the exception path, not about recovering lost context.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
FIXED — branch `fix/8455-failed-call-usage` (worktree `wt-8455`), not yet pushed; the orchestrator
cherry-picks it onto the Gerrit stack.

## Mechanism, re-confirmed at runtime (not just re-read)

The ticket's mechanism held exactly as described. Confirmed by executing it rather than by reading:
a `FunctionModel` whose function raises, driven through the real `PydanticAIRunner.run()` with
`REBAR_USAGE_LOG` pointed at a temp file, raised `LLMUnavailableError` (message preserved, original
`RuntimeError` as `__cause__` — so `interpret_failure` did its job) and left the log file
**non-existent**. That is the live Bedrock 400 reproduced offline in one test.

## Fix — inside `runner.py`'s own `except`, as scoped

`structured_run.py` was off-limits (another agent owns it) and holds `interpret_failure`, so the fix
never touches the spine. Two files:

**`src/rebar/llm/runner.py`** (+6, now 699 LOC) — six lines in `run()`'s own `except` block,
immediately BEFORE `interpret_failure(...)`: `usage_log.record_failure(run_messages, _call_label,
ran_model, req_limit, eff_max_iter)`, plus a WHY comment naming this bug. Nothing else moved; the
success-path `record()` at the end of `run()` is untouched.

**`src/rebar/llm/usage_log.py`** (+77, now 468 LOC) —
* `OUTCOME_OK = "ok"` / `OUTCOME_FAILED = "failed"`, written under an `"outcome"` key on **every**
  row. Explicit on BOTH kinds, per the AC: absence is already this writer's truthful encoding of
  "not applicable" (`model`/`step`/`model_class` are omitted, never nulled), so overloading absence
  to ALSO mean "this call failed" would have made the two unreadable.
* `record()` gains keyword-only `outcome: str = OUTCOME_OK`, so all pre-existing callers are
  behaviourally unchanged. The `not path or not usage` no-op guard is untouched.
* New `record_failure(...)`: resolves `step`/`model_class` off the `step_identity` ContextVar
  (available at failure time exactly as the ticket's live-confirmation comment noted), derives
  counters from `failure_usage(messages, request_limit=…, tool_calls_limit=max(8, eff_max_iter))` —
  mirroring `interpret_failure`'s own `max(8, eff_max_iter)` so the two diagnostics of one failure
  agree — and calls `record(..., outcome=OUTCOME_FAILED)`.

`summarize()` is deliberately **unchanged**: the failure row folds into the totals, which is the
point — the spend total now includes failed calls.

### Never breaking the call path

`record_failure`'s entire body sits in one `try/except Exception` that logs and swallows, not just
the write (which `record()` already guards). This is load-bearing, not defensive habit: its caller
is an `except` block whose one job is to re-raise the provider's exception, so anything escaping
telemetry would REPLACE the real diagnosis. Two tests pin it — the provider error's type, message
and `__cause__` survive, and an unwritable log path degrades telemetry only.

### No double-counting

Three ways, all tested:
1. **One row per `run()` call, not per attempt.** `run_messages` accumulates every internal
   pydantic-ai request/retry attempt, and `record_failure` folds them into a single row. A
   step-budget runaway making N model requests writes ONE row with `requests == N`, not N rows —
   otherwise a runaway's spend would be multiplied by its own step count.
2. **Success and failure paths are mutually exclusive** within one `run()`: the tail `record()` is
   reached only when nothing escaped, and `record_failure` only from the `except`.
3. **A retried call**: the failed attempt's row is `outcome="failed"` and the retry's is
   `outcome="ok"`, so exactly one row is attributable to delivered work. Burned budget is separable
   from delivered work by reading one explicit field.

## Test — RED first, then held out from the implementer

New file `tests/unit/test_usage_log_failed_calls.py` (10 tests). Per the AC every test drives the
real runner with a model that RAISES and then READS the file; nothing asserts on `usage_log.py`
source and nothing exercises `failure_usage()` in isolation. Offline throughout (`FunctionModel` +
`ALLOW_MODEL_REQUESTS = False`), so no billable call.

* **RED confirmed for the right reason:** 7 failed / 3 passed before any fix. The 7 all failed on
  the empty log while the run correctly raised `LLMError`; the 3 that passed are the guard tests
  (no-op-when-unset, error-not-converted, unwritable-sink) which must be green in both states.
* **Held out:** the file was moved OUT of the worktree before the implementation subagent ran; it
  got only a contract card (postconditions + invariants), never the fixture, assertions or path.
  All 10 passed on first re-application — GREEN against an oracle the implementer never saw.
* **Teeth (two defect-seeded mutations):** deleting the `record_failure` call returns exactly the
  original 7 RED; flipping the failure row's marker to `OUTCOME_OK` returns 2 RED — the
  distinguishability test AND the double-counting test, so the marker is genuinely load-bearing and
  not decoration.

## Gates

`make lint` PASS · `make typecheck` PASS (mypy, 407 files) · targeted suites 79 passed
(`test_usage_log`, `test_usage_log_attribution`, `test_usage_log_failed_calls`,
`test_structured_run_seam`, `test_runner_pydantic_budget`, `test_interpret_failure_seam`,
`workflow/test_code_review_usage_attribution`) · full `tests/unit` green · module-size gate clear
(runner 699 / usage_log 468, cap 800 — and runner stays under the 700-LOC headroom target
`test_structured_run_seam` enforces, which is why the helper lives in `usage_log.py`).

## Sibling sweep

None. `usage_log.record` has exactly ONE call site in `src/` (the runner) and it is the one fixed;
this was a single-site defect, not a recurring pattern.

## Note for whoever reads the log next

Rows written before this change have no `"outcome"` key at all. Anything separating delivered work
from burned budget should read `row.get("outcome", "ok")` — a pre-8455 row can only be a successful
call, since a failed one wrote nothing.

compiled_state.description:
# A failed LLM call is invisible in `$REBAR_USAGE_LOG`

## Reported by

`rebar review-code` on change 1178 (story b690), as a medium/correctness advisory finding against
that change. **Verified and confirmed PRE-EXISTING, not introduced by b690** — b690 only added
`step`/`model_class` fields to rows that are written; the omission of failed calls predates it.

## Mechanism (verified by reading the control flow, not inferred)

`PydanticAIRunner.run()` calls `usage_log.record(...)` at the END of the method, AFTER the
`try/except` whose except spine is `interpret_failure(exc, ...)`, and `interpret_failure` ALWAYS
re-raises. So when a model call raises — budget exceeded, provider error, unretryable output,
sampling error — control leaves `run()` without ever reaching `record()`, and NO usage row is
written for a call that may have burned substantial input tokens.

## What this does and does not cost

**Failure spend is not lost entirely.** `usage_log.failure_usage()` builds safe counters (requests,
tool_calls, the four token fields, finish_reason) and `structured_run.py` attaches them as
`exc.diagnostic` at four sites (`:91`, `:100`, `:119`, `:134`), which reach the durable gate-error
sidecar. So the information exists.

**But it never reaches the usage log**, which means:
- a spend total folded from the JSONL by `summarize()` UNDER-REPORTS actual spend, silently, by
  exactly the failed calls. That summary is what the two billable weekly CI jobs
  (`external-integration.yml`, `prompt-eval.yml`) publish to `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY`.
- the per-step attribution added by b690 cannot see failed calls, so "which pass is expensive?"
  is answerable only for calls that succeeded — and a retry-to-exhaustion failure is precisely the
  expensive case an operator would want attributed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] a failed LLM call writes a usage row carrying the same identifying fields a successful one
      does (`op`, `step`, `model_class`, `model`, `provider`) plus whatever token counters are
      known, so a JSONL spend total includes failed calls
- [ ] the row is distinguishable from a successful call (so a reader can separate delivered work
      from burned budget) — the shape is the implementer's call, but it must be explicit, not
      inferred from a missing field
- [ ] asserted by a test in which the model RAISES and the log is then read — not by reading
      `usage_log.py`, and not by asserting on `failure_usage()` in isolation, since the defect is
      about what reaches the FILE
- [ ] the existing no-op-when-unset and `summarize()`-still-folds guarantees still hold
- [ ] telemetry must never break the call path: the record must not convert a provider failure into
      a different exception, nor swallow the original (the existing `record()` already swallows its
      own OSError for this reason — preserve that discipline)
- [ ] no double-counting: a call that fails and is then RETRIED must not be recorded such that the
      same spend appears twice as delivered work

## Note on scope

Not fixed inside b690 deliberately: b690's change is a one-line model-resolution fix plus its
observability prerequisite, and moving `record()` across an exception boundary is a distinct
behavioural change to the failure path with its own double-counting and never-break-the-call-path
risks. Filed under epic 061c because the usage log is that epic's measurement instrument.
compiled_state.title: Usage log omits failed LLM calls: record() sits after run()'s except spine, so a raising call writes no row
